name: Rosa Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you tell me is confidential. I’d like to hear what you’d say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Rosa Torres, twenty-seven. I lead a carpentry crew on building sites, and I live with my partner Luis in a rented flat. We don’t have children; we’re still trying to get our bills under control.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you describe a normal working day, and tell me what you enjoy and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I meet the crew at the site gate before seven, check the plan on paper, and set out who is cutting and who is fitting. I like seeing a clean run of doors hang square because you can tell who took care over the work. The noise and hauling wear me down, but the thing that keeps me alert is wondering if the next job will start on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a computer can help someone read a plan, but it doesn’t make a level wall by itself. If it catches a missing box on the materials list, fine; I still want a person to check what arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes for the cutting and fitting I do every day. I’d still be watching the calendar, because we have less than a month of expenses put away and work nearby is limited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and check every delivery against the paper list. I’d also stop buying lunch on site every day and put that money toward the rent buffer Luis and I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technology part feels small, but money never feels fully settled. I’m not losing sleep over a drawing app; I do worry when the next start date is vague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a computer’s materials list enough to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare it against the order sheet for a few jobs and see whether it misses odd sizes. I wouldn’t let it send the order without the foreman signing off, because a short delivery can leave five people waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the site lost a week of work, what bill would you and Luis cover first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent comes first, then the electricity and the bus cards that get us to work. We would cut takeaways and any clothes we can mend before we fall behind on the rent.

say: I would say a computer can help read a plan, but cannot make a **level wall**.
I’d use a list that catches a missing item, with a person checking every **delivery**.
think: I expect my cutting and fitting work to stay much the same in this **small-change picture**.
I still watch the calendar because our **savings are thin** and local work is limited.
do: Keep leading the **crew** and check each delivery against the **paper list**.
Cut daily site **lunches** and add that money to the rent buffer.
feel: I feel mostly steady about the tool, but **uneasy about work dates**.
S0.quote: I’d say a computer can help someone read a plan, but it doesn’t make a level wall by itself.
fieldNote: Rosa grounds her view in **visible workmanship**, not a general dislike of machines.
Her practical cost cuts reflect a **thin cushion**, even though this scenario barely touches her trade.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew and check deliveries against paper orders
Stop buying lunch on site each day and save that money for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office might send clearer plans and sort the deliveries faster. The crew still needs steady hands to fit timber to an old opening, and I’d want someone responsible to check the drawing before we cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the ordering and checking jobs may change, but I can’t tell from that whether our contractor gets more work or less. There aren’t many sites hiring close to home, so a slow month would hurt even if my own tasks stay hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the foreman to show me the drawing system on a quiet afternoon instead of pretending I know it. I’d keep my crew’s finish work reliable and ask the contractor for the next site date before I commit to extra bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because a quiet spell could cut my pay and there are few nearby crews to ask. I can learn a tool with help, but I don’t like being told that every old way is foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the foreman to check before your crew uses an AI-made drawing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the dimensions checked against the site and the materials list checked against the actual order. A neat screen can still be wrong if the building has been altered since the survey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned scarce local hiring. Would faster ordering itself tell you that fewer sites would open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t say it would reduce starts. The bookings are already uncertain here, and that is why I worry about income; the card doesn’t say there will be fewer projects.

say: I think the office might send **clearer plans** and sort deliveries faster.
A responsible person should check a drawing before our crew **cuts timber**.
think: Changing office tasks do not tell me whether the contractor gets **more work or less**.
Few nearby sites mean a slow month could hurt my **income**.
do: Ask the **foreman** to show me the drawing system during a quiet afternoon.
Ask for the next **site date** before taking on extra bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a quiet spell, though I can learn with someone’s help.
S1.quote: The bookings are already uncertain here, and that is why I worry about income; the card doesn’t say there will be fewer projects.
fieldNote: Rosa distinguishes a known local **booking problem** from an event the scenario never states.
She accepts help with unfamiliar tools but wants a **named person accountable** for checking plans.

steps.text: Keep the crew’s carpentry finish work reliable on each active site
Ask the foreman to teach me the drawing system on a quiet afternoon
Wait for the contractor’s next site date before adding new bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office side of building work will change before the site crew sees a robot. I would tell the crew not to take rumors as a layoff notice, but to ask the contractor what work is actually booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plans and records that come with leading a crew are thinking work, so AGI could take those parts in 2028. The robot date in 2031 reaches the fitting and lifting too; I cannot honestly call carpentry protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working and save whatever I can from each pay, even if it is only a little. In 2029 I’d ask the contractor whether a site crew is still needed and look for another crew if my hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels very short when our savings are less than a month of expenses. I’m anxious about losing hours, although I can still ask the contractor and family what help is possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You might look for another crew, though you expect robots to reach hands-on work in 2031. What could that move solve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could cover a gap in wages while there is still work, but it cannot promise me a permanent place. I’d look because rent is due each month, not because I think another site escapes the same change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours fell in 2029, what would you and Luis decide about your flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d talk through the lease and whether sharing a place with family for a while was realistic. I would not decide in a panic, because moving also costs money and our relatives have their own households.

say: I would tell our crew the office side changes before we see a **site robot**.
I’d ask what work is booked instead of treating rumors as a **layoff notice**.
think: AGI could take the planning and records attached to my **lead role by 2028**.
Robots reach fitting and lifting in 2031, so I cannot call carpentry **protected**.
do: Save what I can from each **pay** while keeping my current crew work.
Ask the **contractor** about crew needs in **2029** and look elsewhere if my hours fall.
Discuss the **lease** and a possible family stay with Luis if hours are cut.
feel: I feel **anxious** because two years is short and our savings cover less than a month.
S2.quote: The robot date in 2031 reaches the fitting and lifting too; I cannot honestly call carpentry protected.
fieldNote: Rosa identifies both **planning tasks** and site work as exposed on the stated timeline.
Her possible family move is a discussion, not a settled plan, because relatives have **their own households**.

steps.text: Save part of each pay toward a household cushion
Ask the contractor about crew needs and apply elsewhere if hours fall in 2029
Discuss the lease and a temporary family stay with Luis

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives a contractor time to show people what is changing and make plans for the crew. I would want the foreman to explain the new process plainly, not send a message after the hours have already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part of my lead job could be taken by AGI in 2031, while robots reach the physical work around 2034. Five years lets me prepare more carefully, but I still depend on construction wages and there are few local employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the foreman to teach me the current digital plans slowly and keep my paper notes beside them until I trust the system. In 2032 I’d check my hours and pay, then speak to other contractors if this crew has lost work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me breathing room, but not a reason to relax about my income. I’m anxious and would want honest notice while I still have wages to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three extra years compared with 2028 let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can build a little more of a cushion and learn one system while someone who knows it is still on the site. I still would not borrow for a long course without knowing there will be work at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider office planning as a safer career after AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, planning and records are exactly the thinking work the card says AGI can do. I’d rather learn the tools I need now than tell myself an office title guarantees wages later.

say: I would say five years gives our contractor time to explain **what is changing** and plan with us.
I want the foreman to speak plainly before the crew’s **hours disappear**.
think: AGI could take the thinking parts of my lead job in **2031**.
More time helps me prepare, but construction wages and **few local employers** still matter.
do: Learn the **digital plans** slowly while keeping paper notes for comparison.
Speak with **other contractors** if this crew loses work.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years gives me more time to save.
S3.quote: I’d rather learn the tools I need now than tell myself an office title guarantees wages later.
fieldNote: Rosa prefers a **patient demonstration** over a rushed software change and wants the foreman beside her.
She rejects office planning as protection because its core tasks are **exposed to AGI**.

steps.text: Learn digital plans beside paper notes with help from the foreman
Build a household cushion from current construction pay
Talk to other contractors if the current crew loses work after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds far away until you count rent payments and jobs that stop between projects. I’d tell my family to take notice of the dates, but not to sell tools or leave work on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use the years before 2036 to save and learn the software in small steps. But AGI can do the planning work and robots follow in 2039, so I don’t know that there will be a safe job waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working and ask the foreman to show me the digital plan tools one task at a time. In 2037 I’d look at my actual hours and pay and ask nearby contractors about openings if work had thinned out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels better than two because I can save in smaller amounts and learn at my pace. I’m still anxious about the end point because my savings are small and the hands-on work changes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to settle with Luis before the 2036 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We should agree how much of my pay can go into savings after rent and food, and whether we want to stay in this flat. We have no children or wedding date, so we don’t need to pretend there’s a family decision already made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a long training course during those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take a short course if the contractor pays and I can see how it helps on the job. I won’t take a loan for a qualification that promises an office career after AGI.

say: I would say ten years sounds long until I count **rent payments** and gaps between jobs.
My family should note the dates, but not leave work on a **guess**.
think: I could save and learn the software in **small steps** before 2036.
I know later robots still threaten my site work, and nobody can promise a **safe job**.
do: Keep working and ask the **foreman** to teach digital plan tools one task at a time.
Check my actual hours and pay in **2037**.
Ask **nearby contractors** about openings if local work thins out.
feel: Ten years feels easier to manage, but I remain **anxious** about the end point.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds far away until you count rent payments and jobs that stop between projects.
fieldNote: Rosa values **gradual learning** and wants training connected to the work she already knows.
Her longer horizon reduces urgency but leaves the **income risk** intact.

steps.text: Keep working on the current crew while construction jobs are available
Learn digital plan tools one task at a time with the foreman
Save what remains after rent and food from each pay
Ask nearby contractors about openings if hours fall after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because it leaves two years to prepare and only about three before robots reach the site work. I’d want the contractor to give clear notice about booked projects and hours, so Luis and I can plan our rent and savings honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a worker is meant to save when a good month still pays lower wages and the next job is uncertain. I want to learn what is useful, but nobody should pretend that wanting to work is the same as having a job.

headlineQuote: I want to learn what is useful, but nobody should pretend that wanting to work is the same as having a job.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** crew lead with a trade certificate and strong carpentry skills.
She lives with her partner Luis, earns lower pay for the job, and has **thin savings**.
She values familiar methods and avoids risk, though she will learn tools when a **trusted foreman** teaches her.
Few similar local jobs make uncertain starts a **real income threat**, even before AI changes the work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries her most because it leaves little time before thinking work changes and robots reach site work.
whatWouldHelp: Clear notice about **booked projects and hours** would help Rosa and Luis plan rent and savings.
